subsection: 3. Empowering people: linking economic growth with human development

notes.b: A country can get richer on paper without its people living better. Empowerment is what connects the two, and it is the idea every later block in this subsection comes back to.
points: Economic growth, a rise in GDP (the total value of goods and services a country produces), does not automatically bring human development, meaning better health, education, freedom and choice.
Growth can be captured by elites, so its benefits stay with a small group instead of reaching ordinary people.
Empowerment means giving people control over resources such as land, credit and income, and a voice in decisions, so that growth actually reaches them.
Empowerment is therefore the link that turns economic growth into human development.
notes.tip: Link every item you write about back to empowerment: say how it lets, or stops, people turning growth into better lives.

notes.b: Many poor countries owe large sums to foreign lenders. The debt built up through a chain of events in the 1970s and early 1980s, and some of the money was badly used.
points: Oil-price rises in the 1970s gave banks large deposits, which they lent to developing countries as “petrodollars” (oil-earned money recycled into loans).

Interest rates soared about 1980 and commodity prices (the prices of raw materials such as coffee and copper) fell, so the loans became far harder to repay: repayments grew while export earnings shrank.
Mexico announced in August 1982 that it could not pay its debts, starting the Latin American debt crisis.
Some loans went to dictators or to prestige projects (grand schemes built for show) that earned no return, so there was no income to repay them.

notes.b: Debt keeps poor countries poor because each stage of the cycle makes the next one worse. Draw it as a loop: debt, reduced spending, poor health and education, low productivity and more borrowing.
points: 1. Debt repayments take up government revenue (the money a government collects), so less is left for everything else.
2. Less is spent on health, schools, water and infrastructure (roads, power and other basic systems).
3. Poor health and education keep productivity (output per worker) and incomes low.
4. Low tax revenue and low export earnings mean the government must borrow more.
5. Debt grows, and the cycle repeats.

To earn the foreign currency needed for repayments, countries push exports of cash crops (crops grown for sale, not food) and raw materials, which can take land from food crops and damage the environment.
notes.tip: A cycle diagram is expected, and each step must be explained, not just listed. Finish by linking the cycle to empowerment: people trapped in it cannot turn growth into better lives.

notes.b: When countries could not repay, lenders offered new loans, but only on strict conditions. These packages were called structural adjustment programmes.
points: Structural adjustment programmes were conditions attached to IMF and World Bank loans in the 1980s and 1990s.

Conditions required governments to cut public spending, privatise state firms (sell them to private owners), open their markets to imports and devalue their currencies (lower their value against others).
Governments were also pushed to introduce fees for schools and clinics and to remove food subsidies (payments that keep food prices low).
The poorest people and women bore most of the cost of cuts to services and subsidies, because they depended most on cheap food and free public services.
Zambia: copper is most of its exports, and its state copper mines (ZCCM) were privatised in the late 1990s as part of reform conditions.
notes.tip: Don't confuse these with tied aid. Structural adjustment conditions are policy conditions on loans, while tied aid must be spent on donor-country goods.

notes.b: Campaigns and international bodies eventually won the cancellation of some debt. The condition was that the money saved had to go on reducing poverty, so the results show debt relief empowering people.
points: The Jubilee 2000 campaign pressed for the cancellation of poor countries’ debts.
The HIPC Initiative (Heavily Indebted Poor Countries) of 1996, run by the IMF and World Bank, offered relief to heavily indebted poor countries.
The Multilateral Debt Relief Initiative of 2005 was agreed after the G8 summit at Gleneagles (July 2005), backed by Make Poverty History and Live 8.
More than 30 countries, most in Africa, received HIPC relief.
Uganda introduced Universal Primary Education in 1997 and in 1998 became the first country to receive HIPC relief; savings went to schools, health and water.
Tanzania abolished primary school fees in 2001, so more children could attend.
Zambia reached HIPC completion point (the stage at which relief is finalised) in 2005 and in 2006 abolished user fees for health care in rural areas.
notes.tip: Use named results such as Uganda, Tanzania and Zambia to show how relief turned into better lives.

notes.b: Debt is rising again in the 2020s. Poor countries that cannot repay are forced into default (failing to pay), restructuring (agreeing new repayment terms) or crisis.
points: Zambia defaulted on its foreign debt in November 2020, the first African default of the COVID-19 period, and later restructured it under the G20 Common Framework.
Sri Lanka defaulted for the first time in 2022; shortages of fuel, food and medicine led to mass protests, and President Gotabaya Rajapaksa fled and resigned in July 2022.
An IMF programme of about 2.9 billion US dollars followed Sri Lanka’s default in 2023.
Ghana defaulted in December 2022, so the wave of defaults was not limited to one country.

UNCTAD (the UN trade and development body; “A World of Debt”, 2023): about 3.3 billion people live in countries that spend more on interest payments than on either health or education, so debt takes money from services that build human development.

notes.h: Chinese lending and the debt-trap debate
notes.b: Not all new debt comes from Western lenders. China has become a major lender, and whether this helps or traps poor countries is disputed.
points: The Belt and Road Initiative, launched in 2013, has channelled Chinese loans to developing countries, mainly for building infrastructure.
Hambantota port, Sri Lanka, was built with Chinese loans and, because the loans were hard to repay, leased to a Chinese state company for 99 years in 2017.
Critics call Hambantota a “debt trap” (lending designed to give the lender control of assets); others argue that Sri Lanka’s debts were mostly owed to Western lenders and bondholders.
notes.tip: Give both sides of the debt-trap debate rather than one.

notes.b: Ireland shows the weight of debt even in a rich country, and what it costs ordinary people.
points: The 2008 crash brought a debt crisis for the Irish state, because the cost of rescuing the banks fell on public finances.
An EU–IMF bailout of €85 billion was agreed in November 2010.
Austerity (tight government spending and higher taxes) brought cuts to services, tax rises and the emigration of young people.
Unemployment rose to about 15% in 2012.
Emigration peaked at about 89,000 in the year to April 2013.
Ireland exited the programme in December 2013.
notes.tip: Don't give Irish national-debt ratios; use the dated facts above.

notes.b: Some argue that debt is not only an economic problem but a question of fairness.
points: Odious debt: loans taken out by a regime and used against its own people are argued to be unfair for the people who must repay them, because they never benefited from the money.

notes.b: Aid is help given to developing countries, but it comes in several forms that differ in purpose, route and conditions.
points: Emergency or humanitarian aid provides food, shelter and medical help after disasters and conflicts.
Long-term development aid funds projects such as water, health, education and farming.
Bilateral aid is given directly from one government to another; multilateral aid is pooled through international bodies such as the EU and UN agencies.
NGO or voluntary aid is channelled through non-governmental organisations (independent, non-profit groups).
Grants are gifts; loans must be repaid, so they add to debt.
Tied aid must be spent on goods or services from the donor country; untied aid can be spent anywhere.
notes.tip: Keep tied aid (money that must be spent on donor goods) separate from conditional loans such as structural adjustment.

notes.b: The UN set a target for how much rich countries should give, but many fall short, and aid levels can swing with donor politics.
points: The UN target of 1970 asks rich countries to give 0.7% of their gross national income (GNI, a country’s total income) as aid.
Norway, Sweden, Luxembourg and Denmark have reached or exceeded the target, so it is achievable; Ireland has not.
The UK cut its aid from 0.7% to 0.5% of GNI in 2021 and in 2025 announced a further cut to 0.3% by 2027.
In 2025 the US government cancelled most USAID programmes (its aid agency) and folded the agency into the State Department; the USA had been the largest single donor by volume.
Aid depends on donor politics: cuts by large donors leave recipients without the funds they had planned for.

notes.b: The case for aid starts with what it does for the people who receive it.
points: Emergency relief saves lives after famine, floods or conflict because it supplies food, shelter and medicine at once.
Schools, clinics, wells and vaccination programmes improve health and education, which means people can work and earn more.
Training and support for women’s groups and small businesses build skills, so incomes rise.
Infrastructure such as roads and power supplies helps local economies to grow because goods and workers can move and businesses can operate.
notes.tip: Exams ask who benefits from aid, so give recipients as well as donors.

notes.b: Aid often serves donor interests as well as recipients, which is the core of the “who benefits?” question.
points: Tied aid returns money to donor firms, because the recipient must buy goods and services from the donor country.
UK aid for the Pergau Dam, Malaysia, was linked to a British arms deal; in 1994 the English High Court ruled that the aid was unlawful because it was not for sound development.
Aid has been used to win political allies, trade deals and influence, as in Cold War aid and in competing offers from China and the EU.
US food aid has long been required by law to be bought largely from US farmers and shipped largely on US ships, so it supports donor farmers and shipping.
Consultants’ fees take a share of aid budgets, so less reaches the people the aid is meant for.

notes.b: Aid can also leave recipients worse off or less able to stand on their own.
points: Corruption and elite capture: aid money can be diverted to powerful groups rather than the poor.
Dependency: recipients can come to rely on aid rather than building their own economies, so they stay vulnerable if it stops.

Cheap imports undercut local producers: in the mid-1990s Haiti cut its tariff (a tax on imports) on rice under pressure from lenders; cheap subsidised US rice flooded in and many Haitian rice farmers were ruined.
In 2010 former US President Bill Clinton publicly apologised for the rice policy, saying it had been a mistake; Haiti is the poorest country in the Americas.
Loans add to debt, and large projects can displace people from their homes and land.
Unsuitable technology can be imposed on communities that cannot maintain it.

notes.b: Writers disagree about whether aid works. Each argument is tied to a named author, which gives you ready examples for an essay.
points: Jeffrey Sachs, The End of Poverty (2005): more aid can end extreme poverty.
Dambisa Moyo, a Zambian economist, Dead Aid (2009): aid breeds corruption and dependency in Africa.
William Easterly, The White Man’s Burden (2006): top-down planners (outsiders who design projects from above) fail, while bottom-up “searchers” (people who find what works locally) succeed.
Effective aid is untied, targeted at the poorest, locally owned, transparent and supports self-help, which answers the main criticisms above.
notes.tip: Exams expect evaluation, so weigh the named arguments against each other rather than listing them.

notes.b: Ireland’s own aid programme is the national example for the aid debate.
points: Irish Aid is part of the Department of Foreign Affairs.
Its bilateral aid programme began in 1974, with partner countries mostly in sub-Saharan Africa, including Ethiopia, Malawi, Mozambique, Tanzania, Uganda and Zambia, and Vietnam.
Ireland’s aid is untied, so recipients are free to spend it anywhere.
“A Better World” (2019) sets priorities: the furthest behind first, gender equality, climate and governance.
Ireland has not reached the 0.7% target.
notes.tip: Don't give euro figures for Irish Aid.

notes.b: The EU is the main international example of an aid donor, and it also shows how other policies can work against aid.
points: The EU institutions and member states together, “Team Europe”, are the world’s largest aid donor, giving over two-fifths of all official development aid.
The Lomé Convention (1975), the Cotonou Agreement (2000) and the Samoa Agreement (signed November 2023) link the EU with the Organisation of African, Caribbean and Pacific States.
ECHO, the EU’s humanitarian aid office (it funds emergency help after disasters), was set up in 1992.
Everything But Arms (2001) is a trade preference (cheaper access to EU markets) for the poorest countries.
Critique: EU farm and fishing policies have at times undermined the same countries.
Global Gateway, launched in 2021, offers up to €300 billion of investment in infrastructure abroad (2021–2027), seen as a response to China’s Belt and Road.
notes.tip: Don't give euro figures for EU aid beyond those above. Here EU aid means aid to developing countries, not EU funds for Ireland.

notes.h: What NGOs are and what they do
notes.b: NGOs are a major route for aid and a major force for empowerment, because they work directly with communities.
points: NGOs are non-profit, non-governmental organisations, funded by donations, governments and the EU, and independent of governments.
They provide emergency relief and long-term development in water, health, education and farming, so they cover both urgent and lasting needs.
They empower communities through co-operatives, women’s groups and microcredit (very small loans for poor people).
They campaign for justice on trade, debt, climate and human rights, so they press governments to change policy, and they run development education in Ireland.
They monitor human rights, so abuses are recorded and publicised.

notes.b: Several Irish NGOs began as responses to a particular crisis or from a particular community.
points: Concern Worldwide was founded in 1968 in response to famine in Biafra, during Nigeria’s civil war, so it began as emergency relief.
Trócaire was founded in 1973 by the Irish Catholic bishops; its Lenten “Trócaire box” funds its work.
GOAL was founded in 1977 by John O’Shea.
Gorta was founded in 1965 as the Freedom from Hunger Council of Ireland and merged with Self Help Africa in 2014.
Self Help Africa was founded in 1984 in response to the Ethiopian famine and supports smallholder farmers (farmers with very small plots).
Bóthar was founded in 1991 in Limerick; it gives farm animals to poor families, who “pass on the gift” of the first female offspring to another family.
Dóchas is the umbrella association of Irish development NGOs.

notes.b: Some NGOs work worldwide, and a few have won the Nobel Peace Prize.
points: Oxfam was founded in Oxford in 1942 as the Oxford Committee for Famine Relief.
Médecins Sans Frontières was founded in France in 1971 and won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1999.
Amnesty International was founded in 1961 by Peter Benenson and won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1977.
The International Committee of the Red Cross was founded in Geneva in 1863, making it the oldest NGO listed here.

notes.b: NGOs have real strengths, but they also have weaknesses that you need to weigh in an evaluation.
points: Advantage: NGOs work close to communities, bottom-up (starting from local people’s needs), at small scale and with appropriate methods.
Advantage: NGOs are fast in emergencies, are not tied to donor trade interests and reach places governments cannot.
Limit: they depend on donations and government grants, so donor priorities shape their work.
Limit: their small scale means they can duplicate or replace state services.
Limit: in 2018 it emerged that some Oxfam staff had used sex workers in Haiti during the response to the 2010 earthquake; Oxfam lost UK government funding for a time and donations fell.
Limit: foreign staff can hold leadership roles that should belong to local people.
Limit: NGOs’ use of negative images of the developing world is criticised. There is more on this in Views of development and underdevelopment.
notes.tip: Exams ask for evaluation, so give both advantages and limits.

notes.b: Land ownership is one of the strongest influences on who gains from growth, especially where most people live by farming.
points: In rural societies land is the main source of food, income, security and status because most people live by farming.
Land can be used as collateral (something pledged to the lender) to obtain credit, so owners can borrow to invest and non-owners cannot.
Who owns the land decides who benefits from growth.

notes.h: Landlords and tenants in nineteenth-century Ireland (national setting)
notes.b: The land system was a major cause of poverty and hunger, though not the only one.
points: The landlord system was built after the plantations: a small, mainly Protestant landlord class, many of them absentee (living elsewhere).
Tenants-at-will had no security and could be evicted; landlords charged rack-rents (very high rents).
Holdings were subdivided into tiny plots, many worked under conacre (land rented for one season to grow a crop) or in rundale (scattered strips held jointly by a group of families).
Dependence on the potato left families exposed to failure of the crop, because they had no other food to fall back on.
The Great Famine of 1845–49 killed about 1 million people and about 1 million emigrated; the state had a population of about 6.5 million (Census 1841).
Causes of the Famine included potato blight, dependence on the potato, the land system and government policy.
The Encumbered Estates Act of 1849 let bankrupt estates be sold, often to new landlords who cleared the tenants.
Emigration followed, so the population fell as families left the land and the country.
notes.tip: Present the land system as a major cause of the Famine, not the only one: blight, dependence on the potato and government policy also mattered. Not all landlords were absentee.

notes.b: Land reform moved tenants from insecurity towards ownership in stages, and the dates matter.
points: The Irish National Land League, founded in 1879 and led by Michael Davitt (from Co. Mayo) and Charles Stewart Parnell, demanded the “Three Fs”: fair rent, fixity of tenure (no eviction while rent is paid) and free sale.

The Land War brought boycotting (shunning someone so completely that they cannot function), so tenants had a weapon without violence; Captain Charles Boycott, land agent at Lough Mask, Co. Mayo, was ostracised in 1880, giving the word “boycott”.
Gladstone’s Land Acts of 1870 and 1881; the 1881 Act granted the Three Fs and set up the Land Commission.
The Ashbourne Act (1885) and the Wyndham Land Act (1903) let tenants buy their holdings with government loans, repaid by annuities (fixed yearly payments).
The Congested Districts Board (1891) improved farms, fishing and cottage industries in poor western areas, because the west had the smallest plots and poorest land.
By the early twentieth century most farmers owned their land; security encouraged investment, but many farms stayed small and fragmented, and the west stayed poor.
Ownership gave tenants security, income and political power, which is how land reform empowered them.
notes.tip: The Wyndham Act was 1903 and the Land League 1879. The 1881 Act gave the Three Fs; ownership came with the Ashbourne and Wyndham Acts, so don't say the Land League won ownership in 1881.

notes.h: Land ownership in Latin America and Africa
notes.b: Unequal ownership, often rooted in colonial history, has held back development in these regions, and badly managed reform can do harm too.
points: Latin America has latifundia (large estates) and minifundia (tiny plots); Brazil has one of the most unequal patterns of land ownership in the world.
The MST (Landless Workers’ Movement), founded in 1984, campaigns for land for landless families.
South Africa’s Natives Land Act of 1913 limited Black South Africans to owning land in reserves of about 7% of the country (later about 13%).
Post-apartheid land reform (reform after the end of white-minority rule) since 1994 has transferred land slowly, so the 1913 pattern has only partly changed.
Kenya’s colonial “White Highlands” reserved fertile highland for European settlers, so the best land was kept from Kenyan farmers.
Zimbabwe’s land seizures from 2000 cut farm output and hyperinflation (prices rising out of control) peaked in 2008: badly managed reform damaged development.
notes.tip: Zimbabwe is a reform that damaged development, so don't present all land reform as positive.

notes.b: Where reform gave farmers secure ownership and was well managed, it raised incomes and human development.
points: South Korea’s land reform began in 1950 and Taiwan’s “land to the tiller” programme in 1953; both gave tenant farmers ownership.
Both reforms raised rural incomes before industrialisation, which gave farmers money to spend and a base for later growth.
Kerala abolished landlord tenancy through land reform implemented from 1970; Kerala has about 94% literacy against about 62% in Bihar (Census 2011), a high level of human development.

notes.b: Women are central to farming but are shut out of owning land, which limits their power to turn growth into better lives.
points: Women do much of the farm work in developing countries but own little land.
FAO figures: women make up about 43% of the agricultural labour force in developing countries but fewer than one in five agricultural landholders worldwide.
Without land, women cannot get credit (since land is the collateral banks ask for) or make farm decisions.

notes.b: Land can also be lost to outsiders today.
points: Large foreign purchases or leases of farmland in poor countries take land that local people depend on for food and income.

notes.b: A co-operative is a business owned by its members, who pool land, labour and capital so that small producers gain strength they could not have alone. Irish farmers and savers built several.
points: Horace Plunkett founded the Irish Agricultural Organisation Society (IAOS) in 1894.
The first co-operative creamery opened at Dromcollogher, Co. Limerick, in 1889.

Dairy co-operatives grew into Kerry Group (which grew from the North Kerry Milk Products co-operative at Listowel, 1972), Glanbia (headquartered in Kilkenny) and Ornua, the dairy co-operatives’ export company behind the Kerrygold brand (launched 1962).
The first Irish credit unions (co-operative savings and loan societies owned by members) were founded in Dublin in 1958; Nora Herlihy was a leading founder.

notes.b: European examples show the co-operative idea spreading from a founding set of principles to large businesses.
points: The Rochdale Society of Equitable Pioneers, in England in 1844, set the principles of modern co-operatives.
Denmark’s first co-operative dairy opened at Hjedding in 1882; co-operatives transformed Danish farming because small farmers gained shared processing and markets.
Arla Foods is today a Danish–Swedish dairy co-operative, which shows the model can grow across borders.

Mondragon, in the Basque Country of Spain, was founded in 1956 by the priest José María Arizmendiarrieta; it is now a federation of worker-owned co-operatives in industry, retail, finance and a university, employing about 70,000 people.

notes.b: In India, co-operatives have empowered small farmers and poor women.
points: Amul, a dairy co-operative founded in 1946 at Anand, Gujarat, was led by Verghese Kurien.
Operation Flood, from 1970, spread the Amul model across India, so small farmers everywhere could sell milk through co-operatives; India is now the world’s largest milk producer.

SEWA (Self-Employed Women’s Association), founded by Ela Bhatt in Ahmedabad in 1972, is a trade union of women in informal work (work with no contract or regular pay) that runs its own co-operative bank.

notes.b: Who makes decisions, and how far people take part, decides whether development empowers them.
points: Top-down decisions are made by governments, MNCs (multinational companies) and international agencies; bottom-up decisions are made by local communities.
The participation ladder runs from being informed, to being consulted, to sharing decisions, to controlling them, so each rung gives people more power.

notes.b: Involving local people is not only fair, it makes development work better.
points: Local knowledge improves projects, because residents know what is needed and what will work.
Projects that people own are maintained after they are built, because the community has a stake in keeping them working.
Participation builds skills and confidence because people learn by taking part in decisions.
It reduces corruption by making decisions open to scrutiny, so officials are harder to bribe in secret.
It gives women and minorities a voice, so their needs are not overlooked.

notes.b: Ireland has several bodies that bring decisions closer to local people, though power remains with central government.
points: County Enterprise Boards, set up in 1993, were replaced in 2014 by 31 Local Enterprise Offices within the local authorities, supported by Enterprise Ireland.
The Local Enterprise Offices support small local businesses with grants, training and mentoring.
LEADER local action groups have operated from 1991; Údarás na Gaeltachta was set up in 1980; public consultation takes place in planning.
Critique: Ireland is highly centralised and local government has few powers.
notes.tip: Local Enterprise Offices replaced County Enterprise Boards in 2014, so don't describe the boards as if they still exist, except when quoting the syllabus term.

notes.b: Developing-world examples show participation working, and people protesting when they are shut out.
points: Porto Alegre, Brazil, began participatory budgeting in 1989, letting residents vote on spending priorities for their districts; many cities worldwide have copied it.
India’s 73rd Constitutional Amendment (1992) set up elected village councils (panchayats), with one-third of seats reserved for women.

The Narmada Bachao Andolan (“Save the Narmada Movement”), led by Medha Patkar, opposed the Sardar Sarovar dam on the Narmada River, which displaced tens of thousands of families without proper resettlement.
The World Bank withdrew its funding for the Sardar Sarovar dam in 1993.

notes.b: Where people cannot take part, decisions serve the powerful instead of the community.
points: Dictatorships and corruption keep decisions away from ordinary people because power and money stay with a few.
MNCs and lenders set conditions, as in structural adjustment, that local people had no say in.
Women are excluded from decisions by custom, so half the community has no say.

notes.b: Exploitation is the opposite of empowerment: people have no control over how they are treated.
points: Exploitation is the unfair use of people or resources for another’s benefit.
It takes forms such as low pay, unsafe work, forced labour and resources taken without a fair return.

notes.b: At the global scale exploitation runs through supply chains, the series of firms and workers that make a product, where profit flows towards the rich and risk falls on the poor.
points: Rana Plaza, Bangladesh, on 24 April 2013 killed about 1,130 garment workers.
Nike was criticised in the 1990s for sweatshop conditions (low pay, long hours, poor safety) in footwear made by contract factories in Vietnam, China and Indonesia.
Value chains for commodities such as cocoa and coffee leave producers with a small share of the final price.
About 160 million children were in child labour in 2020 (ILO and UNICEF).
The DR Congo produces about 70% of the world’s cobalt, and child labour in its mines has been reported by Amnesty (2016).
Niger Delta oil spills in Nigeria were documented by a UNEP study of Ogoniland (2011); Ken Saro-Wiwa was executed in 1995.
MNCs shift profits and tax out of poor countries.
notes.tip: Don't repeat the MNC case study from elsewhere; use exploitation as the empowerment angle.

notes.b: Slavery has not ended: millions of people today are held in conditions they cannot leave.
points: ILO, Walk Free and IOM (2022) estimated that about 50 million people were in modern slavery in 2021: about 28 million in forced labour and 22 million in forced marriage.
Migrant workers in some countries are tied to employers under the kafala system (where a worker’s legal status depends on the employer), which leaves them open to exploitation.

notes.h: Exploitation at the local and national scale
notes.b: Exploitation also happens close to home, in Ireland and in South Asia.
points: Landlords and moneylenders exploited tenants in nineteenth-century Ireland, through rack-rents and eviction.
Bonded labour (work to pay off a debt, with no freedom to leave) in South Asia is illegal in India under the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976, yet persists in brick kilns and on farms.
Caste discrimination (unfair treatment based on birth into a social group) excludes people from better-paid work, so poverty passes down generations.
Ireland’s Atypical Working Scheme for non-EEA crew in the fishing fleet, introduced in 2016 after media reports of exploitation, has been criticised for tying workers to one employer.
Low-paid informal work in cities is another common form of exploitation.

notes.b: Women and children are among those most at risk, because they have the least bargaining power.
points: Women and children are often given the lowest-paid factory jobs because they have the least bargaining power.
Women and children are trafficked (moved by force or deception to be exploited).
Unpaid domestic work is largely done by women, so it earns no income and counts for nothing in GDP.

notes.b: Exploitation can be reduced when workers and consumers gain power, and when laws set minimum standards.
points: Trade unions give workers a collective voice on pay and conditions, because one worker alone has little bargaining power.
Co-operatives and fair trade give producers ownership and a fairer price. There is more on this in Sustainable development as a model for the future.
Ethical consumer campaigns pressure firms to improve conditions because firms fear losing customers.
The Bangladesh Accord, an agreement on safety in garment factories, is one response.
The EU’s supply-chain due diligence law (2024) requires firms to check their supply chains.
ILO conventions (agreements of the International Labour Organization) set minimum standards for labour, so countries that sign agree to a basic floor.

notes.b: Gender roles shape who has money, land and a voice, so they are central to empowerment.
points: Gender roles are the tasks and behaviour a society expects of men and women.
Gender roles differ between and within societies and change over time.

notes.b: Much of women’s work is unpaid, and so does not show up in GDP.
points: ILO (2018): women perform about three-quarters of all unpaid care work worldwide.
In many developing countries women grow much of the food, collect water and fuel and care for children, while men control cash crops and income.

notes.b: Women face a set of linked barriers, each of which holds back their ability to gain from growth.
points: Girls receive less schooling because of early marriage, school fees and household chores.
Women own less land and have less access to credit, because banks ask for collateral such as land.
Women have lower pay and more informal jobs, so they have less income and less security.
Women face maternal health risks, violence and exclusion from decision-making.
After the Taliban returned to power in August 2021, Afghanistan banned girls from secondary school (2022) and women from universities (December 2022), an extreme case.

notes.h: Why empowering women links growth to development
notes.b: Empowering women is a clear case of how empowerment turns growth into human development, because the benefits spread through families.
points: Educated, earning women tend to have fewer, healthier and better-educated children.
Household income spent by women is more likely to go on food, health and schooling.
More women working and running businesses raise GDP.
Kerala shows how women’s education and empowerment go with human development.

notes.b: Microfinance, quotas, campaigns and jobs all aim to empower women, with mixed results.
points: Grameen Bank, Bangladesh, was founded by the economist Muhammad Yunus as a project in 1976 and as a bank in 1983; it lends small sums without collateral, mostly to poor women in groups.
Yunus and the Grameen Bank shared the Nobel Peace Prize in 2006, a sign of how widely microfinance was admired.
Microfinance has limits: in 2010 a microfinance crisis in Andhra Pradesh, India, saw borrowers trapped in multiple loans and reports of suicides, which led to state restrictions on lenders.
SEWA organises women in informal work and runs its own co-operative bank.
Rwanda: women have held over 60% of seats in the lower house since 2013, so women help make national decisions.
Malala Yousafzai was shot by the Pakistani Taliban in 2012 for campaigning for girls’ education; she won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2014.
Ready-made garments make up most of Bangladesh’s exports, and most garment workers are women: the jobs bring independence, but also exploitation, as Rana Plaza showed.
notes.tip: Microfinance is not a cure-all, so give both Grameen’s success and the Andhra Pradesh crisis. Don't quote repayment rates or borrower numbers.

notes.b: Irish gender roles have changed over time, helped by law, and Iceland shows how far equality can go.
points: The marriage bar, which made women in the public service resign on marriage, was removed in 1973, so married women could then keep their careers.
The Electoral (Amendment) (Political Funding) Act 2012 cut State funding to parties unless at least 30% of their general election candidates were women (from 2016), rising to 40% (from 2023).
A record 44 women were elected to the 174-seat Dáil in November 2024, about a quarter of the seats.
Iceland has topped the World Economic Forum’s Global Gender Gap Index every year since 2009.

keyTerms.definition: Giving people control over resources and a voice in decisions, so that economic growth reaches them.
The loop in which debt repayments reduce spending on health and education, which keeps incomes low and drives further borrowing.
Conditions attached to IMF and World Bank loans, such as cutting spending, privatising and opening markets, in exchange for financial support.
A 1996 scheme run by the IMF and World Bank that offered debt relief to heavily indebted poor countries if savings went to poverty reduction.
Debt taken out by a regime and used against its own people, which is argued not to be fairly repayable by those people.
Aid that must be spent on goods or services from the donor country.
Aid given directly from one government to another.
A non-profit, non-governmental organisation that delivers aid, campaigns for justice or both, and is independent of governments.
Large estates in Latin America, owned by a small number of landowners.
A rent set at or near the full value of the land, which tenants could not afford easily.
The Land League’s demands of fair rent, fixity of tenure and free sale of tenants’ interests.
Land rented for one season to grow a crop.
An organisation owned and democratically controlled by its members, who share its profits or benefits.
A process in which residents vote on how part of a city’s budget is spent on their district.
The unfair use of people or resources for another’s benefit.
Forced labour, forced marriage and other forms of enslavement in which people cannot leave their situation.
The tasks and behaviour a society expects of men and women.
Small loans, usually without collateral, made to poor people, mostly women, to start or grow small businesses.

factCards.term: Zambia's debt story: adjustment, relief and default
factCards.definition: Copper is most of its exports; its state mines (ZCCM) were privatised in the late 1990s under reform conditions. HIPC completion point 2005; rural health fees abolished 2006. It defaulted in November 2020 and restructured under the G20 Common Framework.

factCards.term: HIPC debt relief: results in Uganda and Tanzania
factCards.definition: Uganda introduced Universal Primary Education in 1997 and in 1998 became the first country to receive HIPC relief, spending the savings on schools, health and water. Tanzania abolished primary school fees in 2001.

factCards.term: Debt crises of the 2020s: Sri Lanka, Ghana and the UNCTAD figure
factCards.definition: Sri Lanka defaulted in 2022; amid shortages and protests President Gotabaya Rajapaksa fled (July); IMF help (about $2.9 billion) followed. Ghana defaulted in December 2022. UNCTAD: 3.3 billion people live where interest exceeds health or education spending.

factCards.term: Hambantota port and the debt-trap debate
factCards.definition: Built in Sri Lanka with Chinese loans, it was leased to a Chinese state company for 99 years in 2017. Critics call it a Belt and Road (2013) debt trap; others argue Sri Lanka's debts were mostly owed to Western lenders and bondholders.

factCards.term: Aid cuts by big donors: two recent examples
factCards.definition: The UK cut aid from 0.7% to 0.5% of GNI in 2021 and in 2025 announced a cut to 0.3% by 2027. In 2025 the USA, until then the largest single donor by volume, cancelled most USAID programmes and folded the agency into the State Department.

factCards.term: How aid benefits recipients: five ways
factCards.definition: Emergency relief saves lives; schools, clinics, wells and vaccination; training; support for women's groups and small businesses; infrastructure.

factCards.term: Who benefits from aid: three ways donors gain
factCards.definition: Tied aid returns money to donor firms: UK aid for Malaysia's Pergau Dam, linked to an arms deal, was ruled unlawful by the High Court in 1994 as not for sound development. US food aid must largely be bought from US farmers and shipped on US ships. Aid also wins allies.

factCards.term: How aid can harm recipients: the Haiti rice example and others
factCards.definition: In the mid-1990s Haiti cut its rice tariff under lender pressure; cheap subsidised US rice ruined many Haitian farmers, and in 2010 Bill Clinton apologised for the policy. Aid can also be captured by elites, breed dependency, add to debt and displace people.

factCards.term: The aid debate: three named authors and their arguments
factCards.definition: Jeffrey Sachs, The End of Poverty (2005): more aid can end extreme poverty. Dambisa Moyo, Dead Aid (2009): aid breeds corruption and dependency in Africa. William Easterly, The White Man's Burden (2006): top-down planners fail; bottom-up searchers succeed.

factCards.term: EU aid programmes: named parts and one criticism
factCards.definition: Team Europe gives over two-fifths of world aid; Lomé (1975), Cotonou (2000) and Samoa (2023) deals with African, Caribbean and Pacific states; ECHO (1992); Global Gateway (2021), a rival to China's Belt and Road. EU farm and fishing policies have at times harmed the same states.

factCards.term: Irish aid programme: who runs it, since when, and its priorities
factCards.definition: Irish Aid (Department of Foreign Affairs) began bilateral aid in 1974; its aid is untied. Partners are mainly in sub-Saharan Africa, e.g. Ethiopia, Malawi, Uganda. A Better World (2019) priorities: furthest behind first, gender equality, climate, governance. Ireland has not reached 0.7%.

factCards.term: Irish NGOs: six, with founding dates and founders or causes
factCards.definition: Concern Worldwide (1968, Biafra famine); Trócaire (1973, Irish Catholic bishops, Lenten box); GOAL (1977, John O'Shea); Gorta (1965), merged with Self Help Africa (1984, Ethiopian famine) in 2014; Bóthar (1991, Limerick), whose donated animals are passed on.

factCards.term: Four international NGOs: origins and awards
factCards.definition: Oxfam: Oxford, 1942, as the Oxford Committee for Famine Relief. Médecins Sans Frontières: France, 1971; Nobel Peace Prize 1999. Amnesty International: 1961, Peter Benenson; Nobel Peace Prize 1977. International Committee of the Red Cross: Geneva, 1863.

factCards.term: NGOs: three advantages and three limits
factCards.definition: Advantages: close to communities and bottom-up; fast in emergencies; not tied to donor trade interests. Limits: donors' priorities shape their work; they can duplicate or replace state services; scandal, as when misconduct by some Oxfam staff in Haiti emerged in 2018.

factCards.term: Nineteenth-century Ireland: four features of the land system
factCards.definition: A small, mainly Protestant landlord class, many absentee, created after the plantations; tenants-at-will with no security, facing rack-rents and eviction; holdings subdivided into tiny plots under conacre and rundale; dependence on the potato.

factCards.term: The Great Famine and the land: toll, causes and aftermath
factCards.definition: 1845–49: about 1 million died and about 1 million emigrated. Causes included blight, potato dependence, the land system and government policy. The Encumbered Estates Act (1849) let bankrupt estates be sold, often to new landlords who cleared tenants.

factCards.term: The Land League and the Land War: names, dates and demands
factCards.definition: The Irish National Land League (1879), led by Michael Davitt of Co. Mayo and Charles Stewart Parnell, demanded fair rent, fixity of tenure and free sale. In 1880 Captain Charles Boycott, a land agent at Lough Mask, Co. Mayo, was ostracised: hence boycott.

factCards.term: Irish land reform: the Land Acts in order and the outcome
factCards.definition: 1870 and 1881 Land Acts (the 1881 Act gave the Three Fs and the Land Commission); Ashbourne (1885) and Wyndham (1903) Acts let tenants buy with loans repaid by annuities; Congested Districts Board (1891) for the west. Most farmers came to own their land.

factCards.term: Land ownership in Africa: three contrasting examples
factCards.definition: South Africa's Natives Land Act (1913) limited Black ownership to reserves of about 7% of the land (later 13%); reform since 1994 has been slow. Kenya's White Highlands were kept for European settlers. Zimbabwe's seizures from 2000 cut farm output.

factCards.term: Land reform that helped development: three examples
factCards.definition: South Korea (from 1950) and Taiwan's land to the tiller programme (1953) gave tenants ownership and raised rural incomes before industrialisation; Kerala abolished landlord tenancy from 1970 and has about 94% literacy against about 62% in Bihar (Census 2011).

factCards.term: Irish co-operatives: four milestones
factCards.definition: First co-operative creamery at Dromcollogher, Co. Limerick (1889); Horace Plunkett's IAOS (1894); dairy co-ops grew into Kerry Group (from Listowel, 1972), Glanbia (Kilkenny) and Ornua (Kerrygold, 1962); first credit unions, Dublin 1958, with Nora Herlihy.

factCards.term: Co-operatives in Europe and India: five named examples
factCards.definition: Rochdale Pioneers, England (1844); Denmark's first co-operative dairy, Hjedding (1882); Mondragon, Basque Country (1956), about 70,000 workers; Amul, Anand (1946), spread across India by Operation Flood (1970); SEWA, Ahmedabad (1972), a women workers' union with a co-operative bank.

factCards.term: Participation: the ladder and five reasons it matters
factCards.definition: The ladder runs from being informed, to consulted, to sharing decisions, to controlling them. Participation uses local knowledge; projects people own are maintained; it builds skills and confidence; it reduces corruption; it gives women and minorities a voice.

factCards.term: Participation in Ireland: local enterprise and its limits
factCards.definition: County Enterprise Boards (1993) were replaced in 2014 by 31 Local Enterprise Offices in the local authorities, giving small firms grants, training and mentoring; LEADER groups (from 1991); Údarás na Gaeltachta (1980). Critique: Ireland is highly centralised.

factCards.term: Participation in the developing world: three examples
factCards.definition: Porto Alegre, Brazil, began participatory budgeting in 1989; India's 73rd Amendment (1992) created village panchayats with a third of seats for women; Medha Patkar's Narmada Bachao Andolan opposed the Sardar Sarovar dam, and the World Bank withdrew in 1993.

factCards.term: Modern slavery and local exploitation: figures and examples
factCards.definition: Modern slavery (2021): about 50 million (28 million forced labour, 22 million forced marriage). Bonded labour, banned in India in 1976, persists in brick kilns. Ireland's Atypical Working Scheme (2016), set up after exploitation reports, is criticised for tying non-EEA fishing crew to one employer.

factCards.term: Women's work and the barriers they face
factCards.definition: Women do about three-quarters of unpaid care work (ILO, 2018) and are about 43% of farm labour in developing countries but under one in five landholders (FAO). Barriers: less schooling, credit and pay. Afghanistan banned girls from secondary school in 2022.

factCards.term: Why empowering women links growth to development
factCards.definition: Educated, earning women have fewer, healthier, better-educated children; income spent by women goes more on food, health and schooling; more women working and running businesses raises GDP. Kerala shows women's education going with human development.

factCards.term: Microfinance: the Grameen Bank and its limits
factCards.definition: Muhammad Yunus began Grameen in Bangladesh in 1976 (a bank from 1983), lending small sums without collateral, mostly to poor women in groups; Nobel Peace Prize 2006. Limit: in Andhra Pradesh, India (2010), borrowers were trapped in multiple loans.

factCards.term: Gender roles in Ireland: three changes, and the world's most equal country
factCards.definition: The public service marriage bar ended in 1973; a 2012 Act cut State funding to parties with under 30% women candidates (from 2016), then 40% (from 2023); a record 44 women won seats in the 174-seat Dáil (November 2024). Iceland tops the gender gap index.

questions.prompt: Empowering people is a way of linking economic growth with human development. Discuss this statement with reference to national debt and aid programmes.
questions.model: Introduction: growth does not automatically bring human development; empowerment gives people control over resources and a voice in decisions, so growth reaches them. Debt: the origins of the crisis (petrodollar lending, rising interest rates, Mexico 1982); the cycle of poverty, step by step; structural adjustment conditions and their effects on the poor and women; HIPC results in Uganda, Tanzania and Zambia; the 2020s crises in Zambia, Sri Lanka and Ghana; the Hambantota debate; Ireland’s 2010 bailout and austerity. Aid: types of aid; who benefits, including the donor interests shown by Pergau Dam and US food aid; how aid can harm recipients, as in Haiti; the Sachs, Moyo and Easterly debate; Irish Aid as untied bilateral aid; EU aid and Team Europe. Evaluation: debt relief and untied, targeted aid can empower; tied aid and debt dependency can keep growth from reaching the poor.

questions.prompt: Discuss land ownership patterns and their impact on development.
questions.model: Why land matters: food, income, security, collateral and status. Nineteenth-century Ireland: the landlord system, tenants-at-will, rack-rents, conacre and rundale, dependence on the potato, the Great Famine (with its several causes), the Encumbered Estates Act and emigration. Reform: the Land League and the Three Fs, boycotting, the Land Acts of 1870 and 1881, the Ashbourne and Wyndham Acts, the Congested Districts Board; outcome of owner-occupation with small, fragmented farms and a poor west. Co-operatives: Irish creameries and credit unions; Danish dairies; Mondragon; Amul and SEWA. Developing-world examples: Brazil’s concentration and the MST; South Africa and Zimbabwe, where badly managed reform damaged output; South Korea and Taiwan, where reform raised rural incomes before industrialisation; Kerala. Women and land: FAO figures and the barriers to credit. Evaluation: secure, widely held land empowers; concentrated or badly managed land keeps people poor.

questions.prompt: Empowering people is a way of linking economic growth with human development. Discuss this statement with reference to levels of exploitation at local and global scales and differing gender roles in society.
questions.model: Exploitation at the global scale: garment supply chains and Rana Plaza, Nike’s sweatshop criticism, child labour (about 160 million children in 2020), cobalt in the DR Congo, Niger Delta pollution and Ken Saro-Wiwa, and profits shifted out of poor countries. Modern slavery: about 50 million people in 2021. Local and national scale: rack-rents in nineteenth-century Ireland, bonded labour in India under the 1976 Act, caste discrimination, the Irish fishing scheme of 2016. Responses: trade unions, co-operatives, fair trade, ethical consumer campaigns, the Bangladesh Accord, EU due diligence. Gender roles: definition; women’s unpaid care work (ILO 2018); barriers in schooling, land, credit and pay, and Afghanistan’s bans. Why empowering women links growth to development: healthier, better-educated children, household spending on food, health and schooling, and more workers and entrepreneurs. Empowerment in practice: Grameen Bank and its limits (Andhra Pradesh 2010), SEWA, Rwanda’s parliament, the panchayat quotas, Malala Yousafzai, and Bangladesh garment work. Ireland: the marriage bar, the 2012 Act, and the 2024 Dáil. Evaluation: exploitation blocks development and gender barriers waste women’s potential; empowering women and workers makes growth reach people.
